summary: Gives hints and recommendations so an IMAP4 implementation can work with older IMAP2 and IMAP2bis implementations. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Tips so a new mail program can still talk to older ones.

questions: how to detect an imap2 server
subtitle: Hints for making an IMAP4 client or server get along with older IMAP2 and IMAP2bis software.

tldr.problem: IMAP4 was meant to be upwards compatible, but real servers and clients from the IMAP2 and IMAP2bis era behaved differently in a number of small ways.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists IMAP4 facilities and suggests fallback commands for each, explains how to detect an old server with CAPABILITY or trial and error, and notes known incompatibilities for servers dealing with old clients.
tldr.outcome: None of the hints are required by the IMAP4 specification; implementers decide for themselves whether to fail on old software.

today: RFC 1732 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It reflects the state of IMAP implementations in December 1994.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This memo is a summary of hints and recommendations that let an IMAP4 implementation interoperate with implementations of earlier specifications. None of them are required by the IMAP4 specification. The author says the list may be incomplete, since it reflects current knowledge of server and client implementations plus "folklore" gathered as the protocol evolved.

IMAP4 was designed to be upwards compatible, so facilities that were not in earlier specifications should mostly be invisible to a client unless it asks for them. Some older servers may offer "new in IMAP4" capabilities as experimental extensions to the IMAP2 protocol of RFC 1176.
sections.eli5: New mail programs are supposed to still work with old ones. This note collects tips from people who have tried, and none of the tips are rules.

sections.title: Clients Talking to Old Servers
sections.content:
A client can usually find out whether an IMAP2 server supports a facility by trial and error: if the attempt draws a BAD response, assume the server lacks it. A quicker check is the CAPABILITY command. An OK response that includes the IMAP4 capability value means an IMAP4 server. A BAD response, or one without that value, means an older server.

To test for CREATE, DELETE and RENAME, try CREATE INBOX: a NO means the commands exist, a BAD means they do not. Older servers may create a mailbox implicitly when a COPY names a destination that does not exist.

Clients must accept all responses and data formats in the IMAP4 specification, including those labelled obsolete such as the old date and time format, and must not treat a date/time as a fixed-format string. They must not depend on server extensions outside the base specification.
sections.eli5: If you are not sure whether a friend speaks the new language, ask them a simple question first. If they look confused, switch back to the old words.

sections.title: Fallbacks for IMAP4-Only Facilities
sections.content:
The memo gives a fallback for most IMAP4-only features. For example, a client can use LOGIN instead of AUTHENTICATE, SELECT instead of EXAMINE, and the RFC 1176 FIND command in place of LSUB and LIST. For BODYSTRUCTURE it can try the non-extensible BODY item, and for the .PEEK fetch items it can use the plain versions and clear the \Seen flag by hand.

A few features have no workaround at all: the UID fetch item and the UID commands have no equivalent in older servers. The FIND BBOARDS, FIND ALL.BBOARDS and BBOARD commands of RFC 1176 were removed from IMAP4 with no replacement.
sections.eli5: Most new buttons have an old button that does nearly the same job. A couple of new buttons have no old twin, so you just cannot use them with an old machine.

sections.title: Servers Talking to Old Clients
sections.content:
A conforming IMAP4 server and a well-written client for an earlier specification should interoperate, with a few known problems. Earlier wording implied that CHECK is the way to learn the current message count, which is incorrect; a client should remember the latest EXISTS value and avoid needless CHECK commands.

COPY in IMAP4 does not create a missing destination mailbox, which can trip up old clients that expected that. Dates and times changed because of the impending end of the century, so clients that cannot accept a four-digit year or a signed four-digit timezone will not work with IMAP4. Backslash handling in quoted strings also differs, so literals are best when a string contains \ or a double quote. The PREAUTH response is new in IMAP4, but an old client is highly unlikely to see it.
sections.eli5: An old mail program may be surprised by new habits, like four-digit years or a copy command that no longer makes new folders on its own.
